issues.legal_issue: An inam grant evidenced as encompassing both land revenue and the cultivator’s interest includes both interests.
material_facts: The contemporary records showed the inams were granted and enjoyed by the inamdars.
The assessment attributable to the land revenue was too low to provide adequate remuneration for the temple services.
The claimants derived their title from the inamdars on the basis that the inamdars held both interests in the land.
issues.conclusion: The inams comprised both the melwaram and the kudiwaram rights.
issues.legal_principle: The extent of an inam is determined from the grant documents and surrounding evidence, including the manner of enjoyment, the adequacy of the assessment as remuneration, and the basis on which the claimants assert title.

predicates.inam_extent_dispute: The parties disputed whether an inam grant included one or both interests in the land.
predicates.grant_records_show_inam_enjoyment: The grant records showed that the inam was being enjoyed by its holders as an inam.
predicates.assessment_inadequate_for_service_remune: The assessment attributable to the land revenue was too low to adequately remunerate the services associated with the grant.
predicates.claimants_trace_title_to_both_land_inter: The claimants based their title through the inam holders on the premise that those holders had both interests in the land.
predicates.grant_includes_both_land_interests: The inam grant includes both the land revenue interest and the cultivator’s interest.

issues.definition: When the grant records show enjoyment as an inam and the assessment is inadequate for service remuneration or the claimants trace title through holders of both land interests, the grant includes both interests.

issues.legal_issue: An inam granted to hereditary office-holders as remuneration for services connected with a religious institution falls within the statutory resumption scheme, unlike land granted personally subject only to a service condition.
material_facts: The temple trustees appointed persons to perform services connected with the temple and placed the inams in their possession as remuneration for those services.
The inams were confirmed in the names of hereditary office-holders rendering the services, with holders of an office recorded as enjoying shares.
The claimants contended that the inams were personal grants burdened with conditions of service.
issues.conclusion: The inams were granted to office-holders as remuneration for services connected with the temple, rather than as personal inams burdened with a service condition, and were within the scope of the resumption scheme.
issues.legal_principle: There is a distinction between land granted personally subject to a service condition and land granted as remuneration for holding an office. The latter, when the office and services relate to a math or temple, is within section 44-B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926. The Court relied on Forbes v. Noor Mahomed Tuquee and P. V. Bheemsena Rao v. Sirigiri Pedda Yella Reddi.

rule.if: religious_service_inam_resumption_case and office_holders_received_land_as_service_remuneration and services_connected_to_religious_institution and not personal_grant_merely_burdened_by_service

predicates.religious_service_inam_resumption_case: The proceeding concerns whether an inam connected with services to a religious institution may be resumed.
predicates.office_holders_received_land_as_service_: The holders received the land as remuneration for holding offices and performing associated services.
predicates.services_connected_to_religious_institut: The offices and services were connected with a religious institution.
predicates.personal_grant_merely_burdened_by_servic: The land was granted personally to its holder and was merely subject to a condition to perform services.
predicates.office_holder_inam_falls_within_resumpti: An inam granted to an office-holder as service remuneration falls within the resumption scheme.

issues.definition: When office-holders receive an inam as remuneration for services connected with a religious institution, rather than receiving a personal grant merely burdened by service, the inam falls within the resumption scheme.

issues.legal_issue: An alienation made before the enactment of a resumption ground may support a resumption ordered after that enactment where the ground covers alienations already made.
material_facts: The relevant resumption provision was enacted in 1934.
The alienations relied on as grounds for resumption had occurred before 1934.
The resumption orders were made after the provision came into force.
issues.conclusion: The provision authorized resumption after its enactment on the ground of an alienation made before its enactment.
issues.legal_principle: The words “has made” in section 44-B(2)(a)(i) cover past as well as future alienations. The provision operates prospectively because it authorizes resumption after it came into force, even though a condition for that future action may have arisen earlier. The Court relied on Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, 11th edition, page 211.

rule.if: statutory_resumption_case and alienation_predates_resumption_authority and resumption_order_follows_authority and governing_rule_covers_already_made_alienations

predicates.statutory_resumption_case: The proceeding concerns a resumption ordered under a statutory scheme.
predicates.alienation_predates_resumption_authority: The holder made the alienation before the resumption authority came into force.
predicates.resumption_order_follows_authority: The resumption order was made after the resumption authority came into force.
predicates.governing_rule_covers_already_made_alien: The governing rule treats an alienation already made as a ground for resumption.
predicates.prior_alienation_can_support_later_resum: An alienation made before the governing rule came into force can support a resumption ordered afterward.

issues.definition: When a holder alienated the property before a resumption authority came into force, and the governing rule covers already-made alienations, that earlier alienation can support a later resumption.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant cannot rely for the first time on a contention that a lease was only year-to-year when the case previously proceeded on a different account of the alienation and the record supports treating the lease as permanent.
material_facts: The claimants’ pleadings asserted that their predecessor had purchased the lands from the inam holders.
The available direct evidence showed that the predecessor had taken the lands on cowle, meaning lease, from the inam holders.
The claimants and their predecessor had been in continuous possession under that lease for over 80 years and claimed to be permanent alienees.
The claimants first argued in the Supreme Court that the lease was from year to year and therefore did not exceed five years.
The original cowle was not produced, and the record did not support the newly raised contention.
issues.conclusion: The claimants could not raise the year-to-year lease contention for the first time in the Supreme Court; in the circumstances, the cowle was presumed to have created a permanent lease, making the inams resumable on the alienation ground.
issues.legal_principle: A lease falls within section 44-B(2)(a)(i) only if it is for a term exceeding five years; a year-to-year lease does not qualify merely because possession continues for longer. However, a contention contrary to the case pleaded and advanced below may be refused when raised for the first time in the final court, and the character of the lease may be inferred from the record.

rule.if: appeal_from_resumption_order and claimant_first_asserts_short_lease_in_final_court and earlier_case_claimed_purchase_or_permanent_alienation and long_continuous_lease_possession and record_supports_permanent_lease

predicates.appeal_from_resumption_order: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order resuming the property.
predicates.claimant_first_asserts_short_lease_in_fi: The claimant first argues in the final court that the lease was for a short term that would not trigger resumption.
predicates.earlier_case_claimed_purchase_or_permane: In the pleadings or earlier proceedings, the claimant relied on a purchase or a permanent alienation rather than a short-term lease.
predicates.long_continuous_lease_possession: The claimant or predecessor possessed the property continuously for a long period under the lease.
predicates.record_supports_permanent_lease: The record, considered as a whole, supports treating the lease as permanent rather than as a short-term lease.
predicates.lease_treated_as_long_term_alienation: The lease is treated as an alienation for a term exceeding the threshold that permits resumption.

issues.definition: When a claimant first raises a short-lease argument in the final court despite having earlier relied on a purchase or permanent alienation, and the long possession and record support a permanent lease, the lease is treated as a long-term alienation.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee holding through the inam holder does not acquire prescriptive title against that holder merely through continued possession and cannot defeat resumption on that basis.
material_facts: The claimants and their predecessor held the lands as lessees under the inam holders.
Their possession continued under the tenancy and was not adverse to the inam holders.
The claimants argued that their long possession had extinguished the right to resume the lands.
issues.conclusion: The claimants acquired no prescriptive title to the cultivator’s interest against the inam holders, and their possession as lessees did not prevent resumption and dispossession under the statutory scheme. The Court expressed no opinion on whether an alienee could acquire prescriptive title to that interest against the Government through possession that was adverse.
issues.legal_principle: Possession by a lessee during the tenancy is not adverse to the lessor. The claimants therefore acquired no prescriptive title against the inam holders; the Court reasoned that their possession was a fortiori not adverse to the Government under which the inam holders held the land. Section 44-B(2) supplied the resumption authority, and Roman Catholic Mission v. State of Madras was noted as holding that no limitation barred assessment after resumption of the land revenue interest. The Court did not decide whether an alienee could acquire prescriptive title against the Government through adverse possession.

predicates.resumption_proceeding: The proceeding concerns resumption of land held as an inam.
predicates.claimant_possession_derives_from_inam_ho: The claimant possessed the land as a lessee under the inam holder.
predicates.possession_continues_under_tenancy: The claimant’s continued possession remained under the tenancy and was not adverse to the inam holder.
predicates.lessee_acquires_no_prescriptive_title_ag: A lessee whose possession remains under the tenancy acquires no prescriptive title against the inam holder on the basis of that possession.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a resumption proceeding possesses the land as a lessee under the inam holder and continues to possess it under the tenancy, that possession gives the claimant no prescriptive title against the inam holder.
